summary: Mobbin interviews Vitaliy Urban, founder of the astrology app Moonly, about six years and over $1M of A/B tests on onboarding, login, paywalls, pricing and payments. Many winners go against common advice: a 30-screen onboarding built around the user's problem and tailored to the ad they came from, no login screen at all, one consistent paywall instead of contextual per-feature paywalls, realistic images instead of cartoon 3D characters, and no free trial. Small daily tests on every paywall element (images, titles, social proof, fine print, price units) took paid-traffic conversion from 10% in 2020 to 40%. For someone building a design system, it shows which onboarding and paywall patterns to treat as decisions to test rather than defaults, and that imagery style should match who is paying.
key_ideas: A long onboarding (Moonly: 30 screens) is built around the user's job or pain: give a small bite-sized insight, then show how a feature solves the user's specific problem.
Onboarding can be tailored to the ad and App Store page a person came from, so each user job gets its own flow.
Answers collected in onboarding should personalize the first session, including the home screen's quick access buttons.
Ask why an element such as a login screen is needed before copying it from other apps; removing Moonly's login reduced cognitive load.
Contextual paywalls, one per feature, made users think every feature had to be bought separately; one consistent paywall that unlocks everything won.
Paywall images were the biggest lever: a realistic image beat the Disney-style 3D characters the team liked, because paying users over 35 could not see themselves in cartoons.
Personalizing images with the user's own face backfired; people are sensitive to anything involving their face.
Paywall words alone raised conversion by 12%; the guest recommends always adding social proof, and clips from earlier Mobbin guests say a no-commitment fine print line also helps.

A pricey lifetime plan can act as an anchor that raises perceived value; and because people compare prices to each other, not to value, Moonly kept the number and changed the unit (per month to per week).
Free trials can give away the most valuable feature; Moonly removed its trial and uses a one-time offer, usually on day three.
People share insights about themselves, not features, so a one-tap share flow on screenshot drives free reach.
An AI guide giving personal advice needs to feel trustworthy, and a realistic look worked better than cartoon, Disney-like or faceless styles.
Every element, icon and piece of text earned its place by winning a test, and AI tools help run hundreds of tests a month.
Before building an expensive app, validate the market with a lean web funnel.

topics.name: A/B testing and conversion

rules.rule: Build onboarding screens around the user's job or pain rather than the product's features: give a small bite-sized insight, then introduce the feature by showing how it solves that specific problem.
rules.why: Earlier onboardings focused on features instead of the user's problem; the latest version shifted to jobs to be done.
rules.evidence: [0:58] focus to users jobs to be done

rules.rule: When a product has many features, tailor the onboarding flow to the ad or App Store page the user came from, one flow per user job.
rules.why: Not everyone uses each of Moonly's 40 features; custom onboarding flows doubled customer lifetime value.
rules.evidence: [1:22] they tailor the onboarding flow based on the ad you came from

rules.rule: Use the answers collected during onboarding to personalize the first session, including the quick access buttons on the home screen.
rules.why: Customizing the whole experience worked wonders for retention (day one 41%, day 7 37%).
rules.evidence: [2:45] Quick assess buttons on main screen are also customized

rules.rule: Before adding an element seen in other apps, such as a login or sign-up step, ask why the product needs it; Moonly removed login because data was already kept in the Apple keychain and email collection was not paying off.
rules.why: Copying elements from other apps on autopilot adds friction, SMS logins can be slow, and a real email creates cognitive friction; removing login reduced cognitive load.
rules.evidence: [4:02] I always recommend to start with question why

rules.rule: Do not show a different contextual paywall for each feature; show one consistent paywall that makes clear that paying unlocks all features.
rules.why: Every contextual paywall failed Moonly's A/B tests because users thought they had to buy each feature separately.
rules.evidence: [5:36] every single contextual payw wall failed their AB test

rules.rule: Default to a soft paywall the user can close and keep using the app (Moonly shows its close button after 5 seconds), rather than a hard paywall.
rules.why: Across all Moonly's tests the soft paywall won.
rules.evidence: [6:15] Across all our tests, the soft pay wall won

rules.rule: For US users, test a hard paywall.
rules.why: US users are much more accepting of aggressive monetization, and hard paywalls won in the US.
rules.evidence: [6:22] in the US, users are much more accepting of aggressive monetization

rules.rule: Choose paywall imagery the paying audience can recognize themselves in, and test it; for a paying audience over 35, use a realistic style instead of cartoonish 3D characters.
rules.why: The guest feels images are the biggest paywall lever: a single winning image, the first realistic one, delivered a 2x uplift, while the team had fallen in love with a Disney style its over-35 payers could not recognize themselves in.
rules.evidence: [7:16] couldn't recognize themselves in cartoonish 3D characters

rules.rule: Do not personalize product images with the user's own face.
rules.why: Results were inconsistent and some were cringe; people are sensitive to their own face, and thousands avoided opening the app until the feature was removed.
rules.evidence: [7:51] people are sensitive to anything involving their own face

rules.rule: A/B test several variants of the paywall title and subtitle (Moonly tested eight).
rules.why: Changing only the words raised conversion by 12%.
rules.evidence: [8:07] When we only change the words, conversion increased by 12%

rules.rule: Add social proof, such as number of downloads and reviews, to the paywall.
rules.why: The guest recommends always adding it; a clip from an earlier Mobbin guest adds that social accolades show credibility and authority.
rules.evidence: [8:09] I recommend to always add social proof

rules.rule: Add a fine print subtitle such as 'no commitment, cancel anytime' under the paywall offer.
rules.why: A clip from an earlier Mobbin guest (not Moonly) says this subtitle always seems to bump things up incrementally.
rules.evidence: [8:25] This no commitment cancel anytime

rules.rule: Offer a high-priced lifetime plan as a price anchor to raise perceived value and nudge users toward the annual plan over the weekly one, even if it does not sell (on Mobbin, lifetime plans are usually priced at about twice the annual plan).
rules.why: The source says a high-priced lifetime plan can increase the product's perceived value and nudge users toward annual (captions: 'ano') [inferred] over weekly, so it does not need to sell; it calls this price anchoring.
rules.evidence: [9:21] We call this price anchoring

rules.rule: Test keeping the price number and changing its unit, for example 8 bucks per month to 8 bucks a week.
rules.why: People compare prices to each other rather than to value; weekly payments recover ad spend faster. Users who converted at $8 a week churned harder, though the guest says the final total was bigger (captions garbled) [inferred].
rules.evidence: [9:39] we kept the number and changed the units

rules.rule: Do not give away the most valuable feature in a free trial; test removing the trial and showing a one-time offer (Moonly: usually on day three) to users for whom price is the blocker.
rules.why: Trial users felt they got 90% of the value and did not pay; the one-time offer lifted day 3 to day 30 revenue by about 15%.
rules.evidence: [10:44] they removed the free trial completely

rules.rule: When a user takes a screenshot, offer a ready-made flow to share it in one tap, built around insights about the user rather than features.
rules.why: People share insights about themselves; 23% of users share and it brought millions of free views.
rules.evidence: [11:23] takes a screenshot in Moonly, we offer a readym made flow

rules.rule: Give an AI guide that delivers personal advice a realistic visual identity rather than a cartoon, Disney-like or faceless one.
rules.why: People receiving meaningful personal guidance need the entity to feel trustworthy; the other styles did not appeal to users.
rules.evidence: [12:07] they need the entity to feel trustworthy

rules.rule: Have an in-app assistant recommend an add-on only when that specific add-on can really help the user at that moment.
rules.why: Moonly's AI astrologer recommends add-ons only in that case; its in-app announcement system likewise analyses each user's context to anticipate what they might need next.
rules.evidence: [13:02] but only when a specific one can really help user at the moment

rules.rule: On iOS in the US, test offering an alternative to native payments (Moonly uses Stripe) with a small discount.
rules.why: With native payments 50% of cancellations came within 3 minutes of purchase because iOS made cancelling a one-tap habit; adding Stripe doubled LTV overnight and about 80% of US customers now pay with it.
rules.evidence: [13:22] we added Stripe payments as an alternative in the US

rules.rule: Do not offer alternative billing on Android through Google's native SDK.
rules.why: The guest does not recommend it: you control nothing, the interface is designed to scare users away and it lacks Google Pay, which kills almost all conversions.
rules.evidence: [13:44] You can only offer alternative billing with a Google native SDK

rules.rule: Test even the elements people would not usually question, and keep each element, icon and piece of text only after it has won a test.
rules.why: Moonly's paywall went from 10% to 40% conversion through small incremental improvements made almost every day; every element, icon and text earned its place by winning a test.
rules.evidence: [14:39] every element, every icon, every text

rules.rule: Validate the market with a lean web funnel before building the full app.
rules.why: A web funnel gives more freedom and instant market signals; the common mistake is spending millions before learning the market does not exist.
rules.evidence: [15:04] Start with a web funnel

rules.rule: Do not count on App Store featuring to grow a niche app.
rules.why: Featuring brings irrelevant traffic with worse conversion, which can make the algorithm rank the app lower in search; it still works for universal apps like calculators.
rules.evidence: [3:41] it isn't particularly useful for niche apps

rules.rule: Do not assume onboarding must be short; a long onboarding (Moonly: 30 screens) can work when it is built around the user's problem.
rules.why: The usual advice is to keep onboarding short, but Mobbin's study of over a thousand onboarding flows found most top-grossing apps have some of the longest ones, and Moonly takes a similar approach.
rules.evidence: [0:43] on boarding is 30 screens long

rules.rule: Run pricing tests as a priority, testing both the price and the perceived value.
rules.why: The video calls pricing tests the most important experiment you can run in a product, because it comes down to the price and perceived value; Moonly ran 40 in the past year.
rules.evidence: [8:58] Pricing tests are the most important

rules.rule: When running many experiments, use AI tools to match numbers across analytics sources and give a ship, don't ship or collect-more-data recommendation.
rules.why: Moonly runs hundreds of tests a month and says there is no way to manage them manually; it uses Cursor [inferred] and Codex.
rules.evidence: [14:21] AI automatically matches

rules.rule: Personalize the user's avatar by an attribute they gave (Moonly: zodiac sign) to make the product feel more personal, but stop short of using their own face.
rules.why: The guest says the zodiac avatar makes the product feel more personal, while personalizing images with the user's face gave inconsistent, sometimes cringe results and was removed.
rules.evidence: [7:26] personalize users avatar based on their zodiac signs

decisions.question: How long and how tailored should the onboarding be?

options.effect: The usual advice; Mobbin found most top-grossing apps instead have some of the longest onboarding flows.
options.when: Not recommended by this source.

options.name: Feature-focused onboarding
options.effect: Moonly's earlier iterations (three major ones in six years) focused on features rather than the user's problem.
options.when: Replaced by the job-focused version.

options.name: Long, job-focused onboarding (Moonly: 30 screens)
options.effect: Focuses on the user's job or pain, gives an activational insight, then shows the feature that solves it; collects details such as birth details to personalize the first session.

process.step: Start lean with a web funnel
process.detail: Get market signals from a web funnel built alone with AI agents or one front-end developer before building the full app; move slowly and cheaply.

examples.visual_note: A daily guidance card, a moon element (captioned 'moonface', possibly moon phase [inferred]), a personalized daily program, personal transits, and quick access buttons customized from onboarding answers.
A realistic image of a woman at sunset beat Disney-style 3D characters in an A/B test, showing imagery should match the paying audience.
Makes it clear that paying today unlocks all features, in contrast to per-feature contextual paywalls.
Someone searching a specific feature sees a fully customized page and screenshot set; a generic search shows the standard page.
Taking a screenshot triggers a ready-made flow to share the insight in one tap.
An AI guide whose realistic look tested better than cartoon, Disney-like or faceless styles; it also recommends add-on reports when they help.
About 10 production onboarding flows, each built around a job such as anxiety or ADHD.

caveats: Mobbin channel content: it cites Mobbin's own data and earlier episodes and ends with a plug for the channel.

The results come from one bootstrapped astrology app whose paying audience is over 35; the guest and host present them as contradicting common advice, so they are experiments to try, not general rules.
Figures are self-reported by the founder and not independently verified.
The soft paywall still hides its close button for 5 seconds; the guest calls it soft anyway.
The source is inconsistent: the guest says the soft paywall won across all tests, while the host says hard paywalls won in the US.
Payment advice (Stripe in the US, Android alternative billing) depends on platform rules and markets at the time (the guest speaks of 2026) and may date quickly [inferred].

Auto-caption errors: 'payw wall' is paywall, 'Mobin' is Mobbin, 'Only' and 'VR' stand for Moonly and 'their', 'top crossing' is top-grossing, 'Coror' is Cursor; 'niche users toward ano over weekly plan' likely means nudge users toward annual [inferred]; 'final interview ... rebuilds before the scoreboard will die' and 'alternative building conundrate' are garbled; 'cos' likely means cohorts, 'moonface' possibly moon phase, 'payments of Apple' means off Apple, and 'you don't mean to sell' likely means don't need to sell [inferred]; the 'Orbit's' paywall name, 'viculations engine' and 'adaptive drive' are unclear.
Short clips from previous Mobbin guests (social accolades, fine print) are mixed in, so not every line is Vitaliy Urban's.
The source is inconsistent on US payments: the host says Moonly moved US payments off Apple entirely, while the guest calls Stripe an alternative that about 80% of US customers use.
